quiz.title: Definite Integrals by Substitution Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on NCERT Exercise 7.10 — evaluating definite integrals by substitution and changing the limits with the variable. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Put u = 1 + x², so du = 2x dx. Limits change: x = 0 gives u = 1, x = 1 gives u = 2. The integral becomes (1/2) ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> du/u = (1/2) ln 2.

questions.q: When a definite integral is solved by substitution, the neatest method is to:
options: substitute back to x before putting in the limits
change the limits to the new variable and evaluate directly
leave the limits unchanged and hope they still apply
differentiate the answer at the end
questions.explanation: If you switch the limits to the new variable at the same time as the substitution, you never need to return to x. This is the method NCERT uses in Exercise 7.10.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π/2</sup> sin x cos x dx using u = sin x.
questions.explanation: With u = sin x, du = cos x dx. Limits: x = 0 gives u = 0, x = π/2 gives u = 1. So ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> u du = 1/2.
Put u = x², du = 2x dx. Limits: x = 0 gives u = 0, x = 1 gives u = 1. So (1/2) ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> e<sup>u</sup> du = (1/2)(e − 1).

questions.q: If you substitute u = x² + 1, the limits x = 0 and x = 1 become:
questions.explanation: Feed each x-limit into u = x² + 1. x = 0 gives u = 0 + 1 = 1; x = 1 gives u = 1 + 1 = 2. The new limits are 1 and 2.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>π/2</sup> cos x/(1 + sin² x) dx.
questions.explanation: Put u = sin x, du = cos x dx. Limits: x = 0 gives u = 0, x = π/2 gives u = 1. So ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> du/(1 + u²) = tan<sup>−1</sup>(1) − tan<sup>−1</sup>(0) = π/4.
Put u = ln x, du = dx/x. Limits: x = 1 gives u = 0, x = e gives u = 1. So ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> u du = 1/2.
Put u = 1 + x³, du = 3x² dx. Limits: x = 0 gives u = 1, x = 1 gives u = 2. So (1/3) ∫<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> du/u = (1/3) ln 2.

faq.a: It is about evaluating definite integrals by substitution. You replace the variable with a new one, and the key extra step over indefinite integration is that you must also convert the limits of integration to the new variable.

faq.q: Do I need to substitute back to x at the end?
faq.a: No. Once you change the limits to the new variable, you evaluate the integral entirely in that variable. Substituting back to x and then using the original limits also works, but it takes an extra step and is easier to get wrong.

faq.q: How do I change the limits when I substitute?
faq.a: Put each old limit into your substitution formula. For example, if u = x² + 1 and the x-limits are 0 and 1, the new u-limits are 1 and 2. The lower x-limit gives the lower u-limit and likewise for the upper.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in this exercise?
faq.a: Forgetting to change the limits. Students often substitute correctly but keep the original x-limits, which gives a wrong answer. Always update the limits the moment you introduce the new variable.
